units.title: Attention shapes, prefill and decode reuse, and materialized traffic
outcomes: Derive attention shapes and leading matrix-multiply FLOPs for prefill and single-token decode.
Count score and probability storage separately from reads and writes.
Explain why decode has less query-side reuse without declaring it bandwidth-bound from shape alone.
units.why: The score matrix is often larger than the inputs. Its shape explains what tiling removes and why a prefill schedule need not work well for decode.

next.note: Remove the materialized matrices while preserving the attention equation.

study.title: FlashAttention, arXiv:2205.14135v2
study.locator: Section 2.2, Standard Attention Implementation, and Algorithm 0 (p. 4)

study.title: FlashInfer decode shape and layout contract
study.locator: Commit f2794d5, `single_decode_with_kv_cache` docstring: `q`, `k`, `v`, `kv_layout` and `use_tensor_cores` parameters
study.depth: Read the parameter contracts only. Do not implement the production dispatch yet.

focus: For batch size \(B\), query heads \(H_q\), query length \(L\), key length \(S\) and equal key/value head width \(d\), scores have shape \(B \times H_q \times L \times S\). Attention is \(O = \operatorname{softmax}(QK^\top/\sqrt{d})V\), with softmax over keys.

Count the two dense matrix products as \(4 B H_q L S d\) FLOPs, counting each multiply-add as two. Scaling, masking and softmax are additional work. Prefill has many query rows; ordinary decode has one per request.

Algorithm 0 writes and reads both scores and probabilities. At \(b\) bytes per intermediate element this is \(4 b B H_q L S\) requested bytes, not the complete kernel traffic or a hardware-counter measurement.
Decode can reuse each KV head across grouped query heads, but cannot reuse it across a long query tile. Layout, cache residency and schedule determine whether that reuse is realized.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, count noncausal MHA with \(B = 1\), \(H_q = 8\), \(L = S = 1024\), \(d = 64\), and two-byte score/probability storage. The two intermediates occupy 32 MiB and their write-read traffic is 64 MiB; the two matrix products require \(2{,}147{,}483{,}648\) FLOPs. For decode with \(L = 1\) and the same cache, one ideal read of keys and values is 2 MiB. Explain every excluded byte category.
traps: Calling storage size traffic. A tensor may be read several times, and actual memory transactions can exceed requested bytes.
Using the paper's unscaled equation as a different model. Its exposition omits the scale; your reference must include the model's scale.
Assuming the paper's HBM hardware. The same dataflow applies to GPUs with GDDR memory, but bandwidth and on-chip capacity differ.

selfTest.q: Does avoiding the score matrix remove quadratic prefill arithmetic?
selfTest.a: No. Dense attention still computes every allowed query-key interaction. Tiling changes storage and data movement, not the leading dense matrix-product count.

selfTest.q: Why are 32 MiB of intermediates responsible for 64 MiB of requested traffic in this model?
selfTest.a: Each of the two tensors is written once and read once. This excludes input/output movement, repeated tile loads, masks and workspace.

selfTest.q: Does a long KV cache prove decode is memory-bound?
selfTest.a: No. It predicts substantial KV movement. Launches, insufficient parallelism, reductions and address translation may dominate; timing and profiling must distinguish them.

units.title: Online softmax state, query and key-value tiling and output tolerance
outcomes: Derive the running maximum, normalizer and weighted numerator invariants.
Implement a tiled forward pass that retains only query-tile state on chip.
Validate accumulation and rescaling with an independent reference and a stated extreme-value policy.
units.why: Online softmax lets a query row consume keys in pieces. Rescaling both the denominator and weighted numerator is what makes those pieces one attention operation.

next.note: Extend the tiled state to masked rows and shared KV heads.

study.title: Online Normalizer Calculation, arXiv:1805.02867v2
study.locator: Section 3, Algorithm 3 and its induction proof; Section 3.1, equations 3 and 4 (pp. 2 to 4)
study.depth: Stop before Section 4. The proof assumes finite logits; its associativity is a real-arithmetic statement, not bitwise floating-point equivalence.

study.title: CS336 Assignment 2: weighted sum and tiled forward
study.locator: Commit ca8bc81: Section 4.2.1, Example - Weighted Sum, forward pass (pp. 17 to 20); Section 4.2.2, Details of the FlashAttention forward pass and Algorithm 1 (pp. 24 to 25); problem `flash_forward` parts (a) and (b) (pp. 26 to 27)
study.depth: Read the weighted-sum forward example before attention; defer its backward kernel. Start with the public test sizes, not the B200 sweep. Add bounds checks beyond the handout's power-of-two contract.

focus: For processed keys, keep \(m = \max_j s_j\), \(\ell = \sum_j \exp(s_j-m)\) and \(u = \sum_j \exp(s_j-m)v_j\). Output is \(u/\ell\). A rising maximum changes the scale of all old contributions.
For new tile scores \(T\), use \(m' = \max(m,\max T)\), \(a = \exp(m-m')\), \(\ell' = a\ell + \sum_j \exp(T_j-m')\) and \(u' = au + \sum_j \exp(T_j-m')v_j\). Normalize once at the end.
Keep the query tile and row state while streaming key/value tiles. Accumulate reductions and weighted outputs in `tl.float32`; record dot-product precision and casts separately from output dtype.

For finite inputs, compare with a dense double-precision reference using absolute and relative error. Handle empty tiles explicitly. Define all-masked rows as zero output and negative-infinite logsumexp, or reject them; reject NaN and infinite unmasked logits unless you implement another policy.
units.reproduce: Without the source, merge two tiles with logits `torch.tensor([0., 1., 2., 3.], dtype=torch.float64)` and scalar values `torch.tensor([1., 2., 3., 4.], dtype=torch.float64)`, split after the second entry. In PyTorch 2.14.1 the weighted output is approximately 3.492652734585769. Then implement query/key tiling for seed 0 standard-normal inputs of shapes 2 by 17 by 7 and 2 by 19 by 7, with scale \(1/\sqrt{7}\). Both 4 by 5 and 8 by 8 tiles must match the double-precision dense reference within `rtol=1e-12, atol=1e-12` on CPU.
traps: Rescaling the denominator but leaving the old weighted numerator unchanged. A later larger maximum then changes the answer.
Padding keys with zero scores. They still receive probability mass; invalid keys must contribute neither to the normalizer nor the numerator.
Evaluating a difference of two negative infinities for an empty tile. Branch or use safe neutral-state handling rather than letting NaNs enter the recurrence.

selfTest.q: Why can you postpone normalization until the final tile?
selfTest.a: The numerator and denominator share the same running exponential scale. Their ratio is the normalized weighted sum over all keys processed so far.

selfTest.q: Is merging tile states associative?
selfTest.a: For finite logits it is associative in exact real arithmetic: each state summarizes the same weighted exponential sums. Floating-point merge order can change rounding.

selfTest.q: Does subtracting the maximum solve every extreme-value case?
selfTest.a: No. It controls exponential overflow for finite scores, but cannot repair overflow in the dot product or define softmax of an all-masked row. Those need separate contracts.

units.title: Causal and padding masks and MHA, GQA and MQA grouping
outcomes: Implement causal, padding and explicit allowed-entry masks using logical token positions.
Map query heads to shared KV heads without materializing repeated keys and values.
Diagnose diagonal-tile, mask-polarity and rectangular decode errors.
units.why: A fast attention kernel with the wrong mask or head map computes a different model. These bugs often survive square, unpadded tests.

next.note: Optimize the schedule only after its allowed entries are correct.

study.title: FlashAttention-2 mask and head-grouping discussion
study.locator: Section 3.1.1, Causal masking (p. 6), and Section 3.1.2, Multi-query attention and grouped-query attention (p. 7)
study.depth: Correct the reversed inequality in Causal masking item 2: a fully allowed tile has every key position no greater than every query position. The rendered v1 page says the opposite.

study.title: PyTorch 2.14 SDPA mask and GQA contract
study.locator: Equivalent implementation, boolean mask note, GQA constraints, and parameters `attn_mask`, `is_causal` and `enable_gqa`

study.title: FlashInfer packed arbitrary masks
study.locator: Commit f2794d5: Mask Layout (2D Ragged Tensor), through the bit-packing description
study.depth: Use the layout description, not its stale `begin_forward` API example. The pinned implementation uses `plan` and `run`.

focus: Build one allowed-entry predicate from query validity, key validity, request identity, causal positions and any custom mask. Apply it before the maximum and exponential reductions.

For aligned square self-attention, allowed keys satisfy \(j \le i\). For a suffix query block with past length \(p\), the rule is \(j \le p+i\). Do not infer absolute positions from a tile-local index.

For divisible head counts, group size is \(g = H_q/H_{kv}\) and KV head is \(\lfloor h_q/g\rfloor\). MHA has \(g = 1\); MQA has one KV head. Cache storage falls with KV heads, but query-head arithmetic remains.

In SDPA, a boolean `True` means allowed. Its rectangular `is_causal=True` uses upper-left alignment, not automatically the suffix alignment needed by cached decode. Use an explicit mask with `is_causal=False` for the latter.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, implement a CPU reference for four query heads, two KV heads, two suffix queries and five cached keys, all with width 8. Use seed 0 standard-normal `torch.float64` inputs and query positions 3 and 4. Map heads as `[0, 0, 1, 1]`, mask keys after each query position, and compare with PyTorch 2.14.1 SDPA using `attn_mask` and `enable_gqa=True` at `rtol=1e-12, atol=1e-12`. Change one future value and show that the earlier query's output is unchanged.
traps: Treating zero-padded keys as masked. Zero logits still receive probability mass, and padded queries also need an output policy.
Skipping diagonal masking or using strict inequality. A token is allowed to attend to itself in ordinary causal self-attention.
Using the handout's finite sentinel `-1e6` as a universal mask. It is adequate for its random tests, not arbitrary logits; use negative infinity and explicit all-masked handling.

selfTest.q: When can a causal tile be skipped completely?
selfTest.a: When its smallest valid key position is greater than its largest valid query position. A fully allowed tile has its largest key position no greater than its smallest query position. Other tiles need elementwise masks.

selfTest.q: Does four query heads sharing two KV heads halve all attention FLOPs?
selfTest.a: No. Each query head still has its own scores and weighted output. KV-cache capacity is halved relative to four KV heads; traffic savings depend on reuse.

selfTest.q: Why is `is_causal=True` dangerous for a one-row cached-decode query in SDPA?
selfTest.a: Upper-left alignment permits only the first key for that row. If the query is the newest token and all cached keys are valid past tokens, it should attend to the entire cache instead.

units.title: FlashAttention IO complexity and FlashAttention-2 work partitioning
outcomes: Derive the FlashAttention IO bound under its stated two-level memory assumptions.
Explain query-block parallelism and split-query warp ownership in FlashAttention-2.
Predict tile resource limits and distinguish grid parallelism from resident occupancy.
units.why: IO-aware attention is an algorithm plus a schedule. The second paper improves utilization without making dense attention a different mathematical operation.

next.note: Optional: use recomputation to avoid saving quadratic state for training.
Continue the required path with request-local cache layouts and decode.

study.title: FlashAttention IO analysis, arXiv:2205.14135v2
study.locator: Section 3.1, Algorithm 1; Section 3.2, Theorem 2 and Proposition 3; Appendix C, Proof of Theorem 2 (pp. 23 to 24)
study.depth: Skip block-sparse attention. Keep the scope of Proposition 3: it rules out an asymptotic improvement for every memory size in the stated range, not optimality at each fixed size.

study.title: FlashAttention-2 schedule, arXiv:2307.08691v1
study.locator: Sections 3.1.1, 3.2 and 3.3; Algorithm 1 and Figures 2 and 3 (pp. 5 to 9)
study.depth: Algorithm 1 line 10 on the rendered v1 page incorrectly inverts the exponential rescaling. Multiply the old numerator by \(\exp(m_{\text{old}}-m_{\text{new}})\), without an inverse. Use CS336 Algorithm 1 for implementation. Stop before Section 4's hardware-specific results.

focus: In the original square-attention model, \(M\) is fast-memory capacity in elements and \(d \le M \le Nd\). Key/value tiles permit \(\Theta(Nd/M)\) passes over query/output state, giving \(\Theta(N^2d^2/M)\) slow-memory element accesses.

Standard materialization costs \(\Theta(Nd+N^2)\) accesses in this model. Convert elements to bytes using each buffer's dtype; do not insert a shared-memory byte count directly for \(M\). At fixed \(M\) and \(d\), the FlashAttention IO expression is still quadratic in \(N\).

FlashAttention-2 assigns independent query blocks to thread blocks and keeps their state on chip. Within a block, split-query warps own different output rows, avoiding the split-key partial-output combination described in Figure 3.

A tile needs query, key, value, score and output storage, row statistics and compiler temporaries. Larger tiles can reduce reloads but increase registers, spills and shared memory. More blocks in the grid do not guarantee more resident warps.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, derive the IO expression by counting key/value tiles and query/output passes. Draw original key-outer and FlashAttention-2 query-outer schedules, marking every slow-memory read/write and the owner of each output row. For square query tiles of 64 rows with sequence length 1024, batch size 1 and eight heads, derive 128 forward thread blocks. Explain why this grid count is not an occupancy measurement.
traps: Reading 'exact attention' as bitwise equality. The algorithm avoids sparse or low-rank approximation; floating-point order and precision still change outputs.
Treating the IO theorem as a latency prediction. It omits launch overhead, cache hierarchy, exponentials and hardware scheduling.
Confusing split-key warp partitioning with decode's split-KV across thread blocks. They split related dimensions but have different owners, workspaces and merge costs.

selfTest.q: Why does increasing fast-memory capacity lower the modeled IO?
selfTest.a: Larger key/value tiles fit, so fewer outer tiles require fewer passes over query/output state. This says nothing by itself about the best resident tile on real hardware.

selfTest.q: What must split-key workers combine that split-query workers need not combine?
selfTest.a: Contributions to the same output rows. Split-query workers own different rows; split-key workers own different pieces of each row's reduction.

selfTest.q: Why might extra query blocks fail to help one-row decode?
selfTest.a: There is only one query row per head, so query tiling creates no substantial new parallelism. Splitting the KV sequence can create work, but needs a stable state merge and extra workspace.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: the `kernellab` attention IO ledger, schedule diagrams, tile resource budget and prediction checked against timings and compiled resource reports.
units.stopWhen: You derive the IO bound with its assumptions, explain both ownership diagrams, and identify a resource constraint that prevents unlimited tile growth.

fit.note: The two papers cover the IO proof and work partitioning at derive depth; the mini-project supplies the schedule and resource evidence. No new material is needed.

units.title: Backward attention state and recomputation
outcomes: Derive attention input gradients from the rowwise softmax Jacobian.
Reconstruct probabilities from saved logsumexp rather than a saved probability matrix.
Implement the optional backward path and check masks, scale and gradient accumulation ownership.
units.why: This optional unit connects inference-style tiling to training. Recomputing scores can save memory, but correctness depends on preserving the forward scale and mask.

next.note: Compare saved-state memory and full forward-backward boundaries.

study.title: FlashAttention backward derivation, arXiv:2205.14135v2
study.locator: Appendix B.2, Memory-efficient backward pass, and Appendix B.4, Algorithms 3 and 4 (pp. 18 to 21)
study.depth: Use the no-dropout case. Defer random-mask regeneration and a fused GPU backward kernel.

study.title: CS336 backward with recomputation
study.locator: Section 4.2.2, Backward pass with recomputation, equations 13 to 19 (p. 24), and problem `flash_backward` (p. 28)
study.depth: Implement the requested PyTorch backward and compile it. Stop before optional Section 4.2.3. A dense recomputed backward is a learning step, not a memory-efficient tiled backward.

focus: With scaled and masked scores \(S\), save \(L_i = \log\sum_j\exp(S_{ij})\). Reconstruct allowed probabilities as \(P_{ij} = \exp(S_{ij}-L_i)\). Logarithm and exponential bases must agree.

For output cotangent \(G\), compute \(\mathrm{d}P = GV^\top\), \(D_i = \sum_a G_{ia}O_{ia}\) and \(\mathrm{d}S_{ij} = P_{ij}(\mathrm{d}P_{ij}-D_i)\). Then \(\mathrm{d}V = P^\top G\), \(\mathrm{d}Q = \mathrm{d}S K/\sqrt{d}\) and \(\mathrm{d}K = \mathrm{d}S^\top Q/\sqrt{d}\).

Saving inputs, output and one statistic per query row avoids saved quadratic probabilities. A dense backward may still allocate quadratic temporary scores and probabilities; tiled recomputation is needed to remove that peak workspace.

Query-block owners can accumulate query gradients, while key-block owners accumulate key/value gradients. Shared gradient destinations require a reduction or atomics; GQA also sums key/value gradients across query heads in each group.
units.reproduce: From a blank file, implement the no-dropout gradient equations for seed 0 standard-normal `torch.float64` inputs with batch size 2, 17 queries, 19 keys and width 7, and a random output cotangent generated after those inputs. Compare all three gradients against dense PyTorch 2.14.1 autograd on CPU with `rtol=1e-12, atol=1e-12`. Then add causal masking using absolute positions and confirm masked probabilities and their score gradients are zero.
traps: Dropping the score scale in query and key gradients. The softmax score derivative is not yet the derivative of the unscaled dot product.
Using tile-local logsumexp instead of the full row's saved statistic. Reconstructed tile probabilities then normalize independently.
Advertising the compiled dense backward as FlashAttention's tiled memory guarantee. Compilation alone does not prove which quadratic temporaries disappear.

selfTest.q: Why can the row correction be computed from output and its gradient?
selfTest.a: Expanding the output as a probability-weighted sum of values shows that its dot product with the output cotangent equals the probability-weighted sum of probability cotangents. It is one scalar per query row.

selfTest.q: Must recomputation make backward slower?
selfTest.a: No. It adds arithmetic but can remove expensive memory movement. Whether it wins depends on hardware, shape and the actual backward schedule.

selfTest.q: What happens to a shared KV head's gradients under GQA?
selfTest.a: Its key and value gradients are sums of contributions from every query head that uses it, not just one head's contribution.

practice.name: CS336 Assignment 2: `flash_backward`
practice.locator: `test_flash_backward_pytorch` and both causal settings of `test_flash_backward_triton`; run `pytest tests/test_attention.py -k test_flash_backward`

units.title: Variable-length, paged and decode attention
outcomes: Implement request-local ragged indexing and logical-token to physical-page translation.
Build a reduced paged decode path that matches contiguous attention.
Explain when split-KV parallelism needs a stable merge and extra workspace.
units.why: Serving batches contain different lengths and noncontiguous cache pages. Attention must preserve request and token identity while changing storage.

next.note: Write and gather the cache that this address mapping consumes.

study.title: FlashInfer ragged and paged layouts
study.locator: Commit f2794d5: Layout: NHD/HND, Ragged Tensor and Page Table Layout, plus the FAQ on cache ownership
study.depth: Skip MLA and cascade layouts. Read the data contracts rather than copying older API examples. Empty requests need your own policy; the documented last-page rule assumes at least one page.

study.title: Attention states and recursive attention
study.locator: Commit f2794d5: attention-state definition and binary/n-ary merge equations; Applications, KV Sequence Parallelism
study.depth: Apply the merge equations only to disjoint token subsets. Skip shared-prefix performance claims. Use maximum subtraction in the merge, as the text notes but its displayed expression omits.

study.title: Paged decode planning and execution contract
study.locator: Commit f2794d5: `BatchDecodeWithPagedKVCacheWrapper` class example, constructor and `plan`/`run` docstrings
study.depth: Trace one supported backend's shape, page-table and workspace arguments. Do not implement every backend or assume Hopper/Blackwell paths work on Ampere.

focus: Ragged data uses prefix offsets; each request has its own query and KV range. A flat index is not a logical token position, and neighboring requests must never attend to each other.
With page size \(P\), logical token \(t\) uses page-table entry \(\lfloor t/P\rfloor\) and slot \(t \bmod P\). The page-table entry gives the physical page; it need not equal the logical page number.
For a nonempty request with \(n_p\) pages and last-page occupancy \(r\), valid length is \((n_p-1)P+r\), with \(1 \le r \le P\). Read only valid slots, even if stale data occupies the rest.

Split-KV decode produces independent states over disjoint key ranges. Merge normalizers and weighted outputs, not equally weighted partial outputs. Extra launches and partial-state workspace can outweigh the added parallelism.
units.reproduce: From memory, translate a seven-token request with page size 4 and physical page list `[3, 1]`. Its last-page occupancy is 3; token 6 maps to page 1, slot 2. Build a CPU gather oracle, permute the physical allocation while preserving the page table, and verify unchanged dense decode output. Then implement the same mapping in a bounded CUDA or Triton decode kernel with odd lengths and partial pages.
traps: Using allocated page capacity as sequence length. Unused slots are not keys and may contain another request's old data.
Averaging split outputs. Each output is already normalized by a different partition's mass; their logsumexp statistics set the merge weights.
Counting the same prefix in two split states. Merge algebra represents a disjoint partition; overlap double-counts those keys.

selfTest.q: If the last page is full, is its occupancy zero?
selfTest.a: No. It equals the page size. Zero does not encode a full page under the documented nonempty-request contract.

selfTest.q: Should physical page order affect the attention answer?
selfTest.a: No, if the page table still maps the same logical tokens and values. Changing logical token positions or masks would affect it. Floating-point reduction order may introduce tolerated rounding differences.

selfTest.q: Why can splitting the KV sequence help decode when query tiling cannot?
selfTest.a: It creates more independent thread blocks from a long key sequence despite having only one query row. A second reduction combines their attention states, so the gain must exceed that overhead.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: a `kernellab` ragged/paged decode path, a contiguous gather oracle, page-permutation tests, request-isolation tests and split-state checks.
units.stopWhen: Your reduced decode kernel matches the independent contiguous oracle for permuted pages, unequal request lengths, partial last pages and the chosen empty-request policy.

fit.note: Pinned FlashInfer layouts, decode contracts and recursive-state derivation cover the required mechanisms. The mini-project supplies bounded kernel implementation and independent tests.

units.title: Key-value append, gather, layout conversion and quantized loads
outcomes: Implement KV append, gather and layout conversion with explicit slot ownership.
Validate cache writes across page boundaries and preserve untouched entries.
Explain the optional quantized-load contract and check reconstruction error separately from indexing correctness.
units.why: Attention can be correct while reading the wrong generation of a cache slot. Cache updates need position, allocation, stream and scale contracts of their own.

next.note: Keep position-dependent key rotation consistent with cache writes.

study.title: FlashInfer page append and logical positions
study.locator: Commit f2794d5: `get_batch_indices_positions`, `get_seq_lens` and `append_paged_kv_cache`, including its Example and Note
study.depth: Trace the ordinary append operation. Skip MLA and NVFP4 append paths. The caller allocates pages and updates final lengths before append; the append function is not an allocator.

study.title: FlashInfer layouts and optional quantized decode scales
study.locator: Commit f2794d5: `single_decode_with_kv_cache`, `kv_layout`, `q_scale`, `k_scale`, `v_scale` docstrings and the scale applications in its implementation
study.depth: Inspect FP8 scale semantics, not a promise of FP8 acceleration on your GPU. Use a small software dequantization reference for the optional path; no Blackwell-only packed format is required.

focus: Append maps each new row to a request and absolute token position. Check allocation, page capacity and bounds before launch. Two writers must not own the same destination slot.

For each separate cache tensor, `NHD` orders page, token, head, channel; `HND` orders page, head, token, channel. A changed view of strides is not a physical layout conversion. Test gather before and after the actual conversion.
Initialize unused slots to sentinels, append known rows, gather valid tokens and check that all other slots remain unchanged. Preserve stream ordering and keep storage alive until consumers finish.

Optional quantized loads must specify format, reconstruction scale and granularity for keys and values. Per-tensor key scale can enter score scaling and per-tensor value scale can enter output scaling; token- or group-varying scales cannot generally be moved outside those reductions.
units.reproduce: Implement a small append/gather round trip with separate key/value caches, page size 4, two heads of width 3, and a seven-token request on physical pages `[3, 1]`. Fill unused storage with `-99.0`; append increasing integer-valued rows and verify exact gathered values and untouched slots. Convert `NHD` storage to `HND` and repeat. For optional symmetric integer quantization, reconstruct finite unclipped values as \(\hat{x} = s\operatorname{round}(x/s)\) with positive scale \(s\), and check the bound \(\lvert\hat{x}-x\rvert \le s/2\) up to rounding tolerance.
traps: Appending with old last-page lengths or unallocated next pages. The final page metadata must already describe the destination capacity and length.
Overwriting shared prefix pages. A serving allocator needs copy-on-write or an ownership rule before mutable append; the kernel cannot infer that from addresses.
Applying the quantization error bound to clipped outliers. Saturation introduces additional error, and small reconstruction error does not by itself bound attention-output or task-quality error.

selfTest.q: How can an append test detect a write that does not affect today's output?
selfTest.a: Check sentinels in every unowned slot. Otherwise a stray write can remain invisible until that slot is reused or read later.

selfTest.q: Can one output scale represent independently scaled value tokens?
selfTest.a: Not in general. Each token contributes with its own scale inside the weighted sum. Only a common value scale can be factored out.

selfTest.q: Does changing the layout label move the cache data?
selfTest.a: No. The label tells the consumer how to interpret storage. A physical conversion must rearrange data or produce correctly strided storage that the consumer supports.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: `kernellab` KV append/gather and layout-conversion kernels, boundary and sentinel tests, stream-order checks and optional dequantized loads against an independent reference.
units.stopWhen: Append, gather and conversion preserve token identity across partial and full pages, with untouched-slot and bounds checks; any optional quantized path reports clipping and output error separately.

fit.note: The pinned FlashInfer append and decode sources expose position, layout and scale contracts. The mini-project supplies the required write/gather kernels and optional software quantization tests.

Implement half-split and interleaved RoPE with correct request positions.
Choose a legal norm/RoPE fusion boundary and validate it against separate operations.
units.why: Normalization and rotation are small kernels with strict numerical and layout contracts. Fusion is useful only when it preserves their order, reduction domain and positions.

study.title: FlashInfer RoPE positions and pairing layouts
study.locator: Commit f2794d5: `apply_rope` docstring, especially `indptr`, `offsets`, `rotary_dim` and `interleave`

focus: RMSNorm uses \(x/\sqrt{\operatorname{mean}(x^2)+\epsilon}\) before the learned scale. LayerNorm subtracts the mean and uses population variance, not the sample-variance denominator. Neither is a substitute for the other.

Promote low-precision inputs before squaring and reducing. Centered variance avoids subtracting nearly equal raw moments. Mask padded lanes out of both reductions and divide by the valid width, not the padded tile width.

A RoPE pair maps \((a,b)\) to \((a\cos\theta-b\sin\theta, a\sin\theta+b\cos\theta)\). Half-split pairs corresponding entries from two halves; interleaved pairs adjacent channels. Position offsets and frequency conventions are model parameters.

A fused head-norm/RoPE kernel must finish the whole head reduction before rotating and storing pairs. Do not move a model's hidden-width pre-norm through its projection, or reorder learned channel scales and rotation. Test fusion against the exact original operation order.
units.reproduce: Write CPU double-precision references for RMSNorm, centered LayerNorm and half-split RoPE. With input `[3., 3., 3., 3.]`, unit weights, zero LayerNorm bias and `eps=1e-5`, LayerNorm returns zero while RMSNorm does not. For input `[1., 2., 3., 4.]`, rotate half-split pairs by angles 0.3 and 0.7 radians using genuine sine/cosine tables; squared norm is preserved within `rtol=1e-12, atol=1e-12` in PyTorch 2.14.1. Implement the forward GPU kernels and compare fused head-norm then RoPE with the separate reference order.
traps: Using dtype-dependent default \(\epsilon\) in one baseline and a fixed value in another. Pass the same explicit \(\epsilon\) and affine parameters.
Assuming the challenge's randomly generated `cos` and `sin` tables represent unit rotations. Its tests check the algebraic transform, not trigonometric identity or position generation.

Squaring large finite values without a range policy. Float32 promotion prevents many half-precision overflows, not every possible float32 overflow; test or reject inputs outside your supported numerical range.

selfTest.q: Why can padding zeros corrupt LayerNorm even though their input contribution is zero?
selfTest.a: They change the denominator if counted as features. After mean subtraction their squared deviations are also nonzero unless explicitly masked.

selfTest.q: Does norm preservation prove that a RoPE implementation uses the correct layout?
selfTest.a: No. Rotating the wrong pairs can still preserve norm. Compare the model's pairing layout, frequencies and absolute positions with an independent reference.

selfTest.q: Can arbitrary learned channel scales commute with RoPE?
selfTest.a: No. A pair's two scales generally differ, so scaling before rotation and scaling after rotation produce different vectors. Preserve the prescribed order.

units.title: SwiGLU MLP and epilogue fusion boundaries
outcomes: Implement a gated MLP path with the correct projection orientations and activation order.
Fuse a bounded activation or residual epilogue without changing required outputs or dtype boundaries.
Derive removed intermediate traffic and explain reduction and resource limits on larger fusion groups.
units.why: Pointwise fusion can remove launches and intermediate traffic. Fusing a complete MLP or normalization into a GEMM is harder because consumers need completed reductions and different data reuse.

study.title: LeetGPU 84: SwiGLU MLP Block specification
study.locator: Commit 9c9dbe5: `reference_impl`, `get_solve_signature` and `generate_example_test`; inspect `generate_functional_test` before implementing

study.title: FlashInfer residual/RMSNorm mutation contract
study.locator: Commit f2794d5: `fused_add_rmsnorm` docstring, Step 1, Step 2 and parameter contract
study.depth: Read the ordinary fused operation only. Do not enable architecture-specific launch mechanisms or quantized variants for this unit.

focus: The challenge computes \(A = XW_g\), \(U = XW_u\), \(H = \operatorname{SiLU}(A) \odot U\) and \(Y = HW_d\). Its weights use input-by-output orientation, unlike the stored weight of PyTorch's linear module.

A fused pointwise SiLU/multiply kernel can read the two projection outputs and write one hidden tensor. A projection epilogue can remove more traffic only if the needed gate and up results are available to the same owner after their reductions finish.

Residual addition, affine scaling and activation are pointwise after a completed GEMM result. RMSNorm and LayerNorm require a row reduction across all normalized features; one output tile is generally not the entire row.

FlashInfer's fused residual/RMSNorm updates the residual buffer to the sum and the input buffer to its normalized version. Preserve both outputs if the model needs them. Include saved residual writes and changed rounding points in a fusion comparison.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, implement challenge 84's two-row basis-vector example in double precision. The first two columns of both input-by-output projection weights are identity and the other two are zero; the down weight returns the first two hidden features. The output is diagonal with value \(\operatorname{sigmoid}(1)\) and zero off-diagonal entries. Then draw separate, pointwise-fused and projection-epilogue dataflows, counting each removed intermediate write/read at its actual dtype and naming every required output that remains.
traps: Computing SiLU of the elementwise gate/up product instead of multiplying the activated gate by the up projection. These are different functions.
Eliminating a residual write even though the next layer needs the unnormalized residual stream. A removed output is not a legitimate bandwidth saving.
Assuming fewer launches guarantee a faster MLP. Fusion may duplicate GEMM work, spill registers or reduce occupancy, and the down projection still needs its full reduction.

selfTest.q: Why can a pointwise residual epilogue be easier than a norm epilogue?
selfTest.a: Each completed output element needs only its corresponding residual. Norm needs statistics across the entire normalization row, which may span several output tiles.

selfTest.q: Does SwiGLU with zero input return zero here?
selfTest.a: Yes. These projections have no bias, so both branches are zero and the hidden tensor and down projection remain zero. Biased projections would require a different answer.

selfTest.q: Why can fused and unfused outputs differ even with the same mathematical order?
selfTest.a: The unfused path may round intermediate tensors to their storage dtype. A fused path can retain a higher-precision value until the final store; compare against an explicit numerical contract, not bitwise equality.

study.title: Goodput service-level objectives
study.locator: Documentation read 2026-10-13: Arguments, the descriptions of goodput service-level objectives, request rate and maximum concurrency
study.depth: Use the definitions, not a required CLI run. Full production-engine integration belongs to the next section.

focus: Compare the dense correctness oracle, eager SDPA, compiled full block and a supported pinned FlashInfer path separately. Record the actual selected backend, its workspace and any fallback. Failure to support a case is not a zero-latency result.

Start with prefill and one-row decode, then vary batch, sequence, head width, GQA ratio, causal/padding/custom masks, dtype, strides and tile alignment. Include tiny, odd-length and irregular cases; hold some shapes out from tuning.

Warm up compilation and allocator state outside steady-state trials. Interleave variants, retain raw samples and report medians with uncertainty. Profile separate runs; use timelines and compiled resource reports to explain losses rather than infer a bottleneck from achieved bandwidth alone.

Translate local latency using the changed critical-path share. Request TTFT includes more than prefill attention; TPOT excludes the first token and averages remaining request time. Define goodput as successful requests meeting predeclared latency objectives per unit observation time, with the same tokenizer, outputs and arrival workload.
units.reproduce: Derive the serial fixed-workload bound \(S_{\text{end}} = 1/(1-f+f/r)\), where \(f\) is the baseline time share of the replaced operation and \(r\) its local speedup, with all other work unchanged. A hypothetical 20% share and twofold local speedup give \(S_{\text{end}} = 1/0.9\), approximately 1.111, not twofold. Then substitute measured full-block shares and compare the prediction with your bounded prefill/decode runner. Label runner TTFT/TPOT separately from HTTP endpoint metrics.
traps: Benchmarking against only an unfused dense reference. It is an oracle and explanatory baseline, not the strongest performance competitor.
Calling a block's event duration TTFT or goodput. Request metrics need request boundaries, output validation, a workload and service-level objectives.
Improving tokens per second by changing output length, prefix-cache state or quality. Keep those controls fixed, report cache state, and count only validated requests as successful.

selfTest.q: Can reducing peak attention workspace increase serving capacity without reducing one request's latency?
selfTest.a: Yes. It can allow a larger batch or more cached requests. That is a separate capacity experiment; it does not establish lower latency at the original fixed workload.

selfTest.q: Why can mean inter-token latency differ from mean request TPOT?
selfTest.a: They weight observations differently, and one streamed output can bundle several tokens. TPOT amortizes each request's post-first-token duration over its remaining tokens; inter-output gaps are separate observations.

selfTest.q: A custom kernel loses on tiny decode. Is that evidence the implementation is wrong?
selfTest.a: Not by itself. Launch, merge or dispatch overhead may exceed useful work. First validate correctness, then keep the losing case and choose a measured fallback.

selfTest.q: What should you do if a strong baseline wins every tested regime?
selfTest.a: Report the negative result and keep that baseline as dispatch. Do not claim the section's end-to-end gain gate passed; identify a narrower measured bottleneck or leave that gate outstanding.
